### Choosing the latent width The same image can be reconstructed through codes of different widths. In the UvA experiment, the input has $32\cdot32\cdot3=3072$ scalar values; separate models use 64, 128, 256 or 384 latent coordinates. Each model is evaluated on the validation split using the sum of squared pixel errors per image, averaged over images. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/autoencoder-course-2026-11-03/uva-latent-width.svg|Validation reconstruction error for 64, 128, 256 and 384 UvA latent coordinates]] *Original validation-loss plot from Phillip Lippe, [UvA, Comparing latent dimensionality](https://uvadlc-notebooks.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial_notebooks/tutorial9/AE_CIFAR10.html#Comparing-latent-dimensionality). The horizontal axis is logarithmic; the vertical axis uses the summed pixel error, not the error of one pixel. Notebook cell 26, complete original SVG; [MIT](/licenses/uva-c7d9e18f-MIT.txt).* Increasing the code width lowers the measured validation error in this experiment. A plotted point compares separately trained models, rather than turning a single trained model's width knob at inference time. The curve does not establish a universal scaling law or show that every larger model will generalize better. A width of 64 gives 48 times fewer scalar coordinates than the input: $3072/64=48$. That is not a measured 48-fold file compression ratio. Storage also depends on the precision of each coordinate, quantization, entropy coding and how the model parameters are stored. A real compression system must count bits and evaluate distortion after encoding and decoding those bits. ### Reconstruction outside the training distribution A small training loss only constrains the model on the distribution used for training. The UvA notebook also passes random noise and hand-constructed patterns through the CIFAR10 autoencoder. These inputs need no class labels, but they test a different question from reconstruction of held-out natural images. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/autoencoder-course-2026-11-03/uva-noise-reconstruction.svg|Two noise inputs and their reconstructions through the 256-coordinate UvA autoencoder]] *Phillip Lippe, [UvA, Out-of-distribution images](https://uvadlc-notebooks.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial_notebooks/tutorial9/AE_CIFAR10.html#Out-of-distribution-images). Each adjacent pair contains the input followed by its reconstruction. Here the inputs are independently generated noise, not CIFAR10 photographs. Notebook cell 32, complete original SVG; [MIT](/licenses/uva-c7d9e18f-MIT.txt).* The decoder produces broad coloured regions in place of the input's pixel-to-pixel variation. The learned bottleneck and decoder have not preserved the particular noise realization. This example does not prove that every autoencoder rejects noise, or that reconstruction error is a calibrated out-of-distribution detector. ![[00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/autoencoder-course-2026-11-03/uva-pattern-reconstruction.svg|Constant fields, block patterns and colour ramps before and after UvA reconstruction]] *Phillip Lippe, [UvA, Out-of-distribution images](https://uvadlc-notebooks.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial_notebooks/tutorial9/AE_CIFAR10.html#Out-of-distribution-images). Input/reconstruction pairs are placed consecutively, four tiles per row. The inputs are synthetic constant fields, a piecewise-constant block pattern and a two-channel colour ramp. Notebook cell 34, complete original SVG; [MIT](/licenses/uva-c7d9e18f-MIT.txt).* The block boundaries and smooth ramps probe different spatial changes. Reading the pairs requires comparing the same input with its reconstruction, not comparing two unrelated tiles. Together with the loss curve, these examples separate three checks: error on held-out data, preservation of a chosen visual detail, and behaviour on inputs outside the training distribution. ## Image retrieval from autoencoder codes An encoder also supplies a vector for image search. The UvA [Finding visually similar images](https://uvadlc-notebooks.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial_notebooks/tutorial9/AE_CIFAR10.html#Finding-visually-similar-images) section encodes a search corpus once and encodes each query with the same model. It then ranks corpus vectors by Euclidean distance. No decoder is needed during that ranking. Let the query code be $u=(0,0)$ and three corpus codes be $a=(0.1,2)$, $b=(1,0.1)$ and $c=(3,3)$. Their distances from the query are approximately 2.0025, 1.0050 and 4.2426. The nearest result is $b$, followed by $a$. Squaring these distances preserves their order, so an implementation can avoid the square root when only the ranking is needed. For a query batch of shape $[Q,d]$ and a corpus of shape $[N,d]$, `torch.cdist` produces a $[Q,N]$ distance matrix. Selecting the smallest $k$ entries in each row gives indices into the corpus. Those indices must remain aligned with image IDs when loading data in batches or shuffling it. The example below checks the ranking against a direct coordinate-wise calculation. Reconstruction training does not fix the units of the code coordinates. Apply an invertible map $A$ to every code and undo it at the decoder input: $$ \begin{aligned} g'(x)&=A\,g(x),\\ f'(u)&=f(A^{-1}u). \end{aligned} $$ The decoded output is unchanged for every input. For Euclidean search, however, the squared distance becomes $$ \|A(z_i-z_j)\|^2 =(z_i-z_j)^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}A(z_i-z_j). $$ With $A=\operatorname{diag}(10,0.1)$, the first coordinate counts much more and the second counts much less. The transformed codes are $a'=(1,0.2)$, $b'=(10,0.01)$ and $c'=(30,0.3)$. Now $a'$ is nearest: its distance is about 1.0198, while $b'$ is about 10. The reconstruction function can remain exactly the same even though the retrieval order changes. This numerical example illustrates the coordinate ambiguity already encountered in the linear autoencoder/PCA discussion. It is a separate worked calculation, not a result from training the UvA models. ```python import torch retrieval_dtype = torch.float64 query_code = torch.tensor([[0., 0.]], dtype=retrieval_dtype) corpus_codes = torch.tensor([[.1, 2.], [1., .1], [3., 3.]], dtype=retrieval_dtype) distances = torch.cdist(query_code, corpus_codes) manual_distances = (query_code[:, None, :] - corpus_codes[None, :, :]).square().sum(-1).sqrt() torch.testing.assert_close(distances, manual_distances) nearest = distances.topk(2, largest=False, dim=1).indices assert nearest.tolist() == [[1, 0]] coordinate_map = torch.diag(torch.tensor([10., .1], dtype=retrieval_dtype)) new_query = query_code @ coordinate_map.T new_corpus = corpus_codes @ coordinate_map.T new_distances = torch.cdist(new_query, new_corpus) assert new_distances.topk(2, largest=False, dim=1).indices.tolist() == [[0, 1]] def retrieval_decoder(z): return torch.stack((z[..., 0].square(), z[..., 1], z[..., 0] + z[..., 1]), dim=-1) recovered_codes = new_corpus @ torch.linalg.inv(coordinate_map).T torch.testing.assert_close(recovered_codes, corpus_codes) torch.testing.assert_close(retrieval_decoder(recovered_codes), retrieval_decoder(corpus_codes)) print(distances, new_distances, nearest) ``` To evaluate an image-search system, choose queries and relevance judgments for the task, then inspect or measure the returned neighbours. A reconstruction loss does not supply those judgments. Pixel reconstruction may preserve background colour that occupies much of an image, whereas a search task may care about the depicted object. Normalizing vectors or switching to cosine similarity changes the search metric; neither operation follows automatically from the autoencoder objective. An exhaustive distance matrix needs $QN$ entries and $O(QNd)$ arithmetic. Large corpora need batching or a suitable nearest-neighbour index. Those search methods are developed in [[00 Учебник/15 Embeddings, Retrieval и RAG/61 Retrieval — от BM25 до dense и hybrid|the retrieval chapter]]; the representation still has to be evaluated for the intended queries.
